nameStory: Staghorn sumac gets its name from its thick, fuzzy branches that look remarkably like deer antlers covered in velvet. The word 'sumac' comes from the Arabic 'summaq,' which was used to describe these plants that have been valued for their tangy, lemony flavor for centuries.
description: Staghorn sumac is a small tree or large shrub that grows 15-25 feet tall, forming dense colonies through underground runners. It has an open, spreading crown with thick branches that fork like antlers. The most striking features are its large compound leaves (made up of many leaflets) that turn brilliant orange and red in fall, and its dense clusters of fuzzy red berries that persist through winter.

idTips.label: Branches
idTips.description: Thick branches are covered in dense, velvety brown hairs that feel exactly like deer antlers in velvet - this fuzzy texture is unmistakable and present year-round

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large compound leaves have 11-31 toothed leaflets arranged along a central stem, turning spectacular shades of orange, red, and yellow in fall - some of the earliest and brightest fall color

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Dense, cone-shaped clusters of fuzzy crimson berries appear at branch tips in late summer and persist through winter - they feel soft and have a tart, lemony taste when crushed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms spreading colonies of multiple stems from underground runners, creating thickets with an open, irregular crown that looks somewhat tropical

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellowish-green flowers appear in dense, upright pyramid-shaped clusters in early summer, later becoming the red berry clusters

habitat: Staghorn sumac thrives in disturbed areas, roadsides, old fields, and forest edges throughout New England, especially in well-drained soils. You'll often find it colonizing sunny slopes, abandoned lots, and areas where the forest has been cleared. It's particularly common along highways and in suburban areas where it can spread freely.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge late in spring as large, bronze-tinged compound leaves that quickly turn green. Look for the distinctive fuzzy branches even before leaves appear.
seasonality.summer: Dense clusters of small yellowish flowers appear at branch tips in early summer. The large compound leaves create a lush, almost tropical appearance.
seasonality.fall: Among the first trees to change color, staghorn sumac explodes in brilliant reds, oranges, and yellows by early September. The fuzzy red berry clusters ripen and become prominent.
seasonality.winter: Easily identified by the combination of thick, velvety brown branches and persistent clusters of fuzzy red berries at the tips - a striking sight against snow.

funFact: You can make a delicious pink lemonade-like drink by soaking the fuzzy red berries in cold water for 30 minutes and straining out the hairs - Native Americans and early settlers used this 'sumac-ade' as a vitamin C-rich beverage, and it's completely safe unlike poison sumac!
confusionNotes: Despite the name similarity, staghorn sumac is completely unrelated to poison sumac and is totally safe to touch. Poison sumac has smooth (not fuzzy) branches, white berries, and grows only in swamps, while staghorn sumac has fuzzy branches, red berries, and grows in dry areas.
contextualKnowledge: Many people wrongly fear all sumacs because of poison sumac, but staghorn sumac is harmless and actually beneficial. The confusion comes from shared common names - they're in different plant groups entirely. Remember: 'berries white, take flight; berries red, forge ahead.'
compareHints: Staghorn sumac is easily distinguished from its relatives by its distinctively fuzzy branches - smooth sumac has smooth branches (as the name suggests), while shining sumac has a winged stem between leaflets. Fragrant sumac is much smaller with only 3 leaflets per leaf instead of staghorn's 11-31 leaflets.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Shining sumac is much smaller than staghorn sumac and lacks its fuzzy branches, while smooth sumac has completely hairless stems and duller leaves.
Smooth sumac differs from staghorn sumac by its hairless twigs and stems, while staghorn feels velvety-fuzzy.
Fragrant sumac is much smaller and more spreading than its tall cousins like staghorn sumac, which can reach 15-25 feet.
